HYPHEN
JENGA TOWER
JINGLES
SECURE LINE
LONG E
Tough Monday, or maybe I’m tired.

I listen to the radio with some frequency.

(I'm pretty set in my waves.)
ALLATINGLE 🤦🏻‍♀️ That one was just bad.

Nice ride, Jeff and Stephan.
I was hoping to see Brian ENO...
TIL that 64A didn’t always mean what it does today.  According to the web, the word has its roots in Greek and Arabic and originally meant a dry powder to apply to wounds.
It wasn't a particularly long solve, but I spent the whole time feeling like I was being kicked in the particulars. I don't know if that's a compliment or a complaint...
Handel's Hallelujah Chorus. Now that's elevator music. Always gives me a high. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=weFJHtcxJt0

Someone’s got to mention (unironically) that:

They mainly speak Catalan in Barcelona (Note: ESTAR exists in Catalan, too

and

The EENIE counting rhyme originally had a racist word in it (so what?; it doesn’t these days,)
Did the creators think it was Wednesday? Way too hard for Monday, come on

I thought the theme was fun, but I really didn't like that some entrees were reversed and other were not. I wasted a few precious minutes staring at ALLATINGLE wondering what I could've gotten wrong, particularly because I got PI(ZZAJ)OINT first. The cluing of "Uplifting music" was more than a little misleading for me, but overall it was a fun puzzle, even if I spent more time on it than I typically do for a Monday!

Ya know? I don't remember the last time I took an elevator that had music or even muzak piped in. How about you all? Do the NYT elevators play music? How about those of you who work in office buildings or places where the ride up or down is long enough to warrant music? Last time I heard elevator music was in a big old downtown Pittsburgh department store, like Kaufmann's or Horne's, sometime in the 1980s. I remember cuz it was a muzak "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds" but rather well done, and catchy. I wonder what it's like to be a muzak creator, what satisfactions there are, what sources of pride. And who goes to department stores anymore? I kind of miss it. 

I like the relative difficulty for a Monday, and the weird confluence of words that got me imagining a rather ghoulish, gruesome narrative, a story called "Unlawful Repast" involving cannibalism, thus the ice saw for those troublesome but tasty elbows, for ella esta morta as they say in Barcelona, but makes for a tasty stew, a recipe you used your Imac to find, it called on you to add IPAs (or a Sam Adams) and egg; in a while, you took a sample spoonful of this elixir and shouted "Yowzah! Let's eat!"

Mmm, this is good, your guest said, after a very unlawful repast. Who's in there anyway, Kim? Sara? It's left me all atingle. 

You shrugged. "No clue," you said.

"If I WERE a Carpenter," I'd be Karen Carpenter, with the most mellifluous female singing voice ever, and BOSS on the drums to boot. https://youtu.be/NpQRsXrduc8?is=Cv4PhR7OYNDcNNd4 And if I were an ace in crosswords, I wouldn't have blue starred on a Monday, for heaven's sakes. I fat-fingered it and an S went in where an A should have been in the crossing of DATA and EAT. I guess I might have caught it if I'd flyspecked, but I don't worry about streaks so it doesn't matter. Obviously :-) I adored this musical puzzle! And I got a nice chuckle out of "uplifting tunes" for ELEVATOR MUSIC. Very well done, Jeff and Stephan. Thank you, gents!

I had never heard of LOEWE bags but, apparently, it is a fine leather design company since 1846 and on their website you can buy a handbag for as low as $5000.00!

I'll take two!

Good puzzle.  Tough by Monday standards, twice my Monday average.

LOEWE and ERRAND BOY crossed with REPAST?  What the heck is a REPAST?  That corner felt more like a Wednesday or Thursday.

I cannot tell you how disappointed I am after I excitedly filled in dANDB (before I had the rest of 7D filled in), only to realize one of my most listened to genres of late was not, in fact, getting some love in the NYT.

I jest, this was a great puzzle! A little more difficult than a typical Monday for my particular sets of knowledge, but fun and rewarding nonetheless.
What's not to like?  Tidy Monday with a clever twist in the theme.
Fun theme, seems comparatively chewy for a monday.  But then I had to go back after solving to figure out what RAN DB was, so maybe it's just me.  Thumbs up either way.
Northeast corner ruined the experience for me.

Northwest with ELBOWS / LOEWE / WISE / REPAST all in the same small section is 100% Friday or Saturday level.

I feel like the Great Easening includes a little psyop they’re using to train newbs with early week puzzles. They seem to be adding sections that are tougher than early week puzzles from years past. Archive Mondays and Tuesdays feel easier to me.

If it’s all about daily active users + average time per session, this would make sense.

Longer sessions in the app, plus training newcomers to battle through the tough bits so they’ll be more likely to give late-week puzzles a try.

I’m just along for the ride, man. Come what may.
As a handbag enthusiast LOEWE was not even my first guess until I got the L in the northeast corner!
Why did you call Stepan "Warnock"? His last name is Prock.

I took the Across only challenge and i made it!! I completed the puzzle in 11:59 without ever looking at any of the Down clues. 

I got lucky because I spotted the theme early, which helped me to fill in some of the fill. I loved it, especially “Jabbers on a plane”!

But in a crossword all about ambient music, where was Brian Eno, who is practically a human Oreo in crosswordland?

"If I were a carpenter and you were a lady, would you marry me anyway, would you have my baby?"  Sounds like a lot of puzzlers are not familiar with this song.  It's not The Carpenters.  Tim Hardin wrote and recorded it in 1966, and Bobby Darin had a hit with his cover in 1967.

I enjoyed this puzzle.  The column puzzled me.  I don't know how anyone but NYT employees and the puzzle constructors know the theme before they start to the puzzle.  Sundays excepted because the theme is given.   Other days, sometimes you figure the theme out while doing the puzzle, sometimes not til you are done.
Challenging northeast corner. Clever theme and execution. Congrats to the authors!
Always a please to see a Jeff Chen et al construct

I needed Tuesday time to fill the grid, mostly because of a distinctly un-Monday-ish NE corner. I ended up having to take a peek at the answer key, too. I don't know what a gofer is, and while I didn't understand what ERRAND BO[w]S might be, the entry didn't look like gibberish, so I accepted it. That [w] came from [w]OWZAH, which seemed perfectly fine! These slangy American expressions are among the most challenging puzzle content for me - there are just so many of them, they all seem quite strange, and they come in a zillion spelling variants on top of it.

How common is elevator music in the US? I hear it very rarely in Poland.
Crunchy for a Monday—I’ll take it.
A Jeff Chen I actually liked

I managed to finish under my average despite hunting a typo for a while. I was convinced it had something to do with the randb?, ran db?, rand b?, genre that I was oblivious to. Finally found and fixed errandboyD, and still managed to finish under my average. :)

Looked up randb afterwards, and boy did I feel dumb. :p
feels more like a tuesday to me!! great solve :)

YOWZAH! When did my teenage ROCK become ELEVATOR MUSIC?

Ugh, one of the signs of aging.

No, you don't often hear music on elevators anymore, but I think of elevator music more generally as the bland-ified music played in the background at any business venue, like supermarkets or other stores  or even as telephone call hold  music. It used to be music from your parents' generation. Oops.

Circles on a Monday! Fun puzzle.

Took me a minute on Sam's column photo. That's a bin full of Meyers lemons.
Is it Tuesday already?

If I am allowed to be picky, based on the revealer clue, "Uplifting music," shouldn't have all the solutions have read from bottom UP to top?  I get that an elevator goes up and down, but the clue alludes to only one direction. Still, a fun puzzle.

Usually when the theme answers are downs, it’s for a reason, and often that theme will be about up-ness or down-ness.  I don’t remember a down-theme-answer grid being about both, as today’s is.  

It made for a splendid moment, actually.  I had filled in the two western theme answers, but not the revealer, and saw LATIN going down and ROCK going up.  I stopped right there trying to figure out the connection between both words and why they were going in opposite directions.

And getting nowhere.  Eventually, I uncle-d, and solved on, and when I uncovered ELEVATOR MUSIC, man, that brought a huge “Hah!”, one of those you hope for in a crossword, but don’t often get.

Props and high thanks for that, Jeff and Stephan!  

By the way, this ELEVATOR MUSIC theme is simple, yes, and you’d think it would have been done before, but I haven’t found it, and I’ve looked.

So, high scores for originality.  Bang up job, you two, and thank you for brightening my day!
Very hard for a Monday, so a bit disappointed. Monday’s are for cruising, not being flummoxed. Some of the clues like “some gofers”,really?

I got stuck in the upper right...and a few other places.

That's not how *I* spell EENEY....actually, I never use that.  I come from a "One potato, two potato" family.

I had gotten KIMONO and KIM, which gave me hope that there would be more words with K*I*M--such as aKIMbo.  Oh, well.

ODESSA is how I've always seen it spelt.  Happy Monday and Happy Labor Day.

Finally a puzzle dedicated to The Love Boat!

The first hint was the circled answers that rose and dipped, evoking the motion of a ship asea.

The definitive proof was the inclusion of "gofer", the valiant purser(Hi, Loewe) of the ship.

And then we have all the allusions to The Odyssey which famously dictated the story arc(not ark) of the series:

-The Sirens tried to lure the sailors to their demise on the ROCKs.
-The Odyssey was written in LATIN or some other ancient gibberish.
-Whenever a crew member asked how much longer the voyage would be, Odysseus answered either "NO CLUE" or "IN A WHILE"(but in Latin or whatever).
-ODESSA!!!!!

The central down answer reinforced the theme, because what song is more elevating than The Love Boat theme song? Set a course for adventure indeed.

Did you know that The Love Boat cruised along for 10 seasons just as Odysseus's voyage took 10 years? (Because men and asking for directions.)

But in the end Odysseus was reunited with his beloved Penelope on Fantasy Island.

CHICK COREA crossing KIM and ODESSA was just inexcusable for a Monday. A very disappointing puzzle whose theme and clues both caused me to frown into my Monday morning coffee.

Very little wordplay, a lot of opaque answers (REPAST? YOWZAH? LOEWE?), and the theme was inscrutable even after solving. A good theme is like a good joke: if you have to explain it, it probably wasn’t all that great. Not a great start to the week.

The plurals of Japanese loan words are the same as their singular form. You do not add an “s” to sushi, kimono, obi, torii, tatami, etc. when pluralizing them.

Japanese nouns are all innately uncountable, and you have to add context. We already do this in English with words like “fish” or “them”, saying “I saw thems” is not really understandable without context, so we say “I saw all of them” or “I saw many of them”.

I understand it’s hard to use those words as plurals when the crossword clues demand (on Mondays, at least) that the plural is obvious, but it’s not right to just make up pluralizations that do not exist

@sotto voce If I Were a Carpenter is also the name of a wonderful tribute album released in the mid-1990s.  Highlights include Shonen Knife taking "Top of the World" to pop-punk heaven, and Sonic Youth's abrasive but compassionate cover of "Superstar".

Anorexia was not seen as a serious eating disorder at the time she melted away.  It's an illness, not just a refusal to eat in order to stay thin. If she had received treatment, she would very likely have continued her career and we would have been able to enjoy her beautiful voice for far longer.

@dutchiris

Yeah, she was gone before I had really internalized the term anorexia.

Strangely, the first time I heard "anorexia" was someone asking me if I had it.  I lost about 75 pounds or so in Grad School, and was borderline anorexic.  I had a lot of the symptoms (excessive/compulsive calorie counting, notebooking my food intake, unable to miss a day of exercise without extreme guilt).  But I was male.

And it was unusual for males at the time to be flirting with disaster like that.  And yet never once did I feel like I was on the edge, even though I was a 5'10" male weighing 130 pounds.  I cringe when I see pictures of myself from that time.

I guess that's part of why the Karen Carpenter story hits me so hard.
